title: Solar Ovens and Clean Cooking
summary: How solar ovens use black surfaces, clear lids, and shiny reflectors to cook with sunlight, and why smoke-free cooking matters for the health of millions of families.
poll: Every home in a sunny country should own a solar oven.

versions.title: Cook with the Sun
versions.text:
Can the sun cook your lunch? Yes, it can! You just need a sun oven.

A sun oven is a box. The box is black on the inside. Black things get hot in the sun. The lid is clear. Light gets in. The heat stays in. The lid helps trap the heat.

The box has shiny flaps. The flaps reflect the light. They bounce more sun into the box. The box gets very hot. It can cook rice. It can bake bread.

Lots of homes cook on a fire. They burn wood. Wood fires make smoke. Smoke is bad for our lungs. Kids and moms breathe it in each day. It can make them sick.

A sun oven makes no smoke. It needs no wood. The sun is free.

A sun oven is slow. It can not cook at night. It needs a clear sky. Saudi Arabia has lots of sun. That makes it a good place for sun ovens.

A solar oven does have problems. It is slow, and it can not cook at night or on a cloudy day. Saudi Arabia gets lots of sunshine, so it is a great place for solar ovens.

versions.title: Solar Ovens and Clean Cooking
versions.text:
Can sunshine cook your lunch? It certainly can. You just need a solar oven. The word solar means "of the sun," so a solar oven is an oven powered by sunlight instead of gas, wood, or electricity.

One common design is a box oven. Its inside is painted black, because dark surfaces absorb sunlight and turn it into heat. A clear glass or plastic lid lets sunlight in but traps the heat, much like a car parked in the sun. The walls are packed with insulation, such as cardboard or wool, which keeps the heat from escaping.

Shiny flaps called reflectors stand around the box. They bounce extra light inside. A good box oven can reach more than 100 degrees Celsius, which is hot enough to cook rice, stew, and bread.

Around the world, many families still cook on open fires that burn wood, coal, or other fuel. Smoke from these fires fills homes with pollution. Breathing it every day can damage the lungs, and it harms millions of people, especially women and children.

Solar ovens make no smoke. Sunlight is a renewable source of energy, which means it will not run out. Families also save money and do not have to cut down trees for firewood.

Solar ovens do have limits. They cook slowly and cannot work at night or on cloudy days. Saudi Arabia, however, gets strong sunshine on most days of the year.

versions.title: Solar Ovens and the Fight for Clean Cooking
versions.text:
Can sunshine cook a meal? It certainly can, with the assistance of a solar oven, which is powered by sunlight rather than by gas, wood, or electricity.

The most common design is the box oven, which combines several simple ideas. Its interior is painted black, because dark surfaces absorb sunlight and convert it into thermal energy, or heat. A transparent lid allows sunlight to enter but prevents most of the heat from escaping, much like a car parked in direct sunlight, while insulation in the walls slows the loss of heat even further. Shiny reflectors around the box direct additional sunlight inside, so a well-built box oven can reach more than 100 degrees Celsius.

A parabolic cooker works differently. It uses a curved, bowl-shaped mirror to concentrate sunlight onto a single point, where a pot sits. Because the light is focused so tightly, a parabolic cooker can boil water or fry food much faster than a box oven, although it must be turned regularly to follow the sun.

Solar cooking is not a new idea. In the 1760s, the Swiss scientist Horace-Bénédict de Saussure built an insulated wooden box with several layers of glass on top, and he discovered that the temperature inside became high enough to cook fruit, which showed that sunlight alone could be used for cooking.

These inventions matter because more than two billion people still cook on open fires or simple stoves that burn wood, charcoal, or animal dung. The smoke fills homes with pollution and causes serious respiratory illnesses, which affect the lungs and breathing. Women and children, who often spend the most time near the fire, suffer the most harm. In some regions, gathering firewood also takes hours each day and contributes to the loss of forests.

Solar cooking is sustainable, because sunlight is free, renewable, and produces no smoke. However, solar ovens cook slowly and cannot work at night or under heavy clouds. Saudi Arabia, which receives intense sunshine on most days of the year, is an excellent location for them.

versions.title: Solar Ovens and the Fight for Clean Cooking
versions.text:
Can sunshine alone cook a good, hot meal for a whole family? It certainly can, with the assistance of a solar oven, which is powered by sunlight rather than by natural gas, firewood, charcoal, or electricity.

The most widespread design is the box oven, which combines several straightforward scientific principles: its interior is painted black, because dark surfaces absorb sunlight efficiently and convert it into thermal energy. A transparent lid permits sunlight to enter but prevents most of the heat from escaping, much like a vehicle parked in direct sunlight on a summer afternoon, while insulation in the walls reduces heat loss even further. Reflective panels surrounding the box redirect additional sunlight into the cooking chamber, so a well-constructed box oven can achieve temperatures above 100 degrees Celsius.

A parabolic cooker operates differently, since it employs a curved, bowl-shaped mirror to concentrate sunlight onto a single focal point, where a blackened pot is carefully positioned. Because the radiation is focused so precisely, a parabolic cooker can boil water or fry food considerably faster than a conventional box oven, although it must be adjusted regularly to track the sun's movement across the sky.

Solar cooking is not a recent innovation. During the 1760s, the Swiss scientist Horace-Bénédict de Saussure constructed an insulated wooden box covered with several layers of glass, and he discovered that the temperature inside became sufficiently elevated to cook fruit, which demonstrated that sunlight alone could be harnessed for culinary purposes.

These inventions are significant because more than two billion people still prepare food over open fires or rudimentary stoves that burn wood, charcoal, or animal dung. The resulting smoke fills homes with pollution and contributes to serious respiratory illnesses, which affect the lungs and breathing, and women and children, who frequently spend the most time near the fire, experience the greatest harm. In certain regions, gathering firewood also consumes several exhausting hours each day for entire families and accelerates the destruction of forests.

Solar cooking is environmentally sustainable, because sunlight is free, renewable, and generates no smoke, although solar ovens cook comparatively slowly and cannot operate at night or beneath heavy cloud cover. Saudi Arabia, which receives intense, reliable sunshine on most days throughout the year, is therefore an exceptionally suitable location for them.

checklist: I explained how each cooker turns sunlight into heat.
I gave one advantage of each design using evidence from the article.
I used precise words such as concentrate, thermal, and insulation.
HIGH.modelAnswer: A box oven and a parabolic cooker both use sunlight, but in different ways. The box oven absorbs sunlight with its black interior and traps the heat using insulation and a clear lid, which slowly builds up thermal energy inside. A parabolic cooker instead uses a curved mirror to concentrate sunlight onto a single point, so it can boil water or fry food much faster than a box oven. One advantage of the box oven is that it is simple and holds heat steadily for slow cooking, while an advantage of the parabolic cooker is its speed, since the focused light heats food quickly. Both designs offer a sustainable alternative to fires that cause respiratory illness from smoke.
